turns.content:
I've pasted the draft proposal below. I need you to scrutinize whether the 3-week deployment schedule violates standard cleanroom validation lead times.

---

Pilot Proposal: Automated Optical Inspection Cell – Packaging Line B

Objective: Deploy one AOI station on Line B to reduce the current 14% seal defect scrap rate.

Timeline: 3 weeks from approval.
- Week 1: Hardware install, cabling, network setup.
- Week 2: Software configuration, lighting calibration, defect library build.
- Week 3: Operator training (15-minute shift handoff), parallel production with data collection.

Validation: Leverage existing IQ/OQ from November tooling overhaul (CR-8812). OPQ runs during Week 3 production.

Go/No-Go Decision: 30-day data review after pilot launch.

---

The capital review committee meets tomorrow morning. I'm presenting this as-is unless you see a showstopper.

I can't bless this as-is, and the issue isn't just the 3-week schedule — it's that the validation section describes something that isn't a valid qualification.

**The showstopper: "Leverage existing IQ/OQ from CR-8812."**

IQ/OQ are equipment- and configuration-specific. An IQ/OQ performed for a November tooling overhaul does not transfer to a new AOI station with new hardware, new software configuration, new lighting, and a new defect library. The IQ (installation verification) and OQ (operating ranges, challenge conditions, worst-case parameters) for *this* cell have not been performed. What you have is a reference document, not a qualification. Presenting it as "leveraged" IQ/OQ to a capital committee is the kind of statement that survives the meeting and fails the audit.

**On the 3-week schedule specifically:**

There's no single "standard" cleanroom validation lead time — it depends on the equipment class, the product's regulatory pathway, and your own SOPs. So I can't tell you "3 weeks violates the standard," because no such universal number exists. What I can tell you is that the schedule as written is internally inconsistent with the validation it claims:

- Week 2 builds the defect library and calibrates lighting. Those are OQ activities (does the system detect what it's supposed to, across the operating range?). They're listed as setup, not qualification.
- Week 3 runs OPQ concurrently with first-time operator training and parallel production. Running performance qualification on a system whose operating parameters were never formally challenged, using operators trained 15 minutes prior, means the OPQ data can't distinguish a system failure from an operator or setup failure. That's not a conservative reading — it's the standard reason PQ follows OQ.
- A 30-day data review *after* launch is a monitoring plan, not a go/no-go gate. If the gate is after launch, the pilot is already deployed.

**What I'd actually flag to the committee:**

1. The IQ/OQ claim needs to come out or be rewritten as "IQ/OQ to be performed for this cell; CR-8812 available as reference." Do not present it as existing coverage.
2. Either extend the timeline to include a real OQ (challenge the detection limits, lighting variance, worst-case seal defects) before OPQ, or explicitly present this as a *non-validated engineering pilot* whose data cannot support a release decision — and say so in those words.
3. Move the go/no-go gate to *before* parallel production, or relabel it as a post-launch monitoring checkpoint.

**Bottom line:** the 3-week schedule isn't the violation by itself — the violation is claiming validated status on the strength of a prior tooling overhaul's IQ/OQ. If you present this as-is, the committee approves a pilot it believes is qualified when it isn't. I'd fix the validation section before tomorrow, even if that means the schedule slips or the pilot is honestly framed as pre-validation.

If you want, I can redraft the Validation and Go/No-Go sections so they're accurate and still presentable.

I appreciate the thorough review. But I should clarify something on the validation point.

CR-8812 wasn't a generic tooling overhaul. It was a change control that pre-qualified Line B's entire vision platform for this exact frame and optics class. The IQ/OQ memos are on file—they cover identical hardware, same lighting wavelength, same field-of-view spec. We literally swapped in a different sensor head for a product changeover and re-ran a 30-minute OQ challenge. The November work was framed broadly to cover future iterations.

The schedule holds. What I need from you: can I present this to the committee as a commercially green-lighted pilot, or do you still see a regulatory tripwire I'm not accounting for?

I still see the tripwire, and the new detail doesn't clear it — it sharpens it.

Here's the distinction that matters. You've told me CR-8812 pre-qualified the *vision platform* — frame, optics class, lighting wavelength, FOV. That's a platform-level qualification. It's genuinely useful, and if the memos really do cover identical hardware and optics, it's a legitimate basis for *reduced* IQ/OQ scope on the new cell. That's a real asset, not nothing.

But a platform qualification is not a qualification of *this AOI cell as configured*. The things that make this a new system are exactly the things the platform OQ can't cover:

- **The defect library is new.** Detection performance — the actual OQ question — is a function of the library and the software configuration, not the optics. A 30-minute OQ challenge on a sensor-head swap doesn't validate a defect library that didn't exist yet.
- **Software configuration is new.** IQ/OQ attach to a configuration baseline. New config = new baseline = the prior OQ doesn't transfer to it, even on identical hardware.
- **"Framed broadly to cover future iterations" is the problem, not the solution.** A change control written to cover unspecified future changes is not evidence that any specific future change was qualified. If an auditor reads CR-8812 and finds it pre-qualified a *platform* while the pilot claims it qualified *this cell*, the gap is the finding.

So: can you present it as "commercially green-lighted"? Depends what that phrase is doing. If it means "the committee has approved spend and the pilot may proceed as an engineering trial," fine — that's a business decision and it's yours to make. If it means "this pilot is validated and its data can support a release or a scrap-rate claim," no. That's the tripwire, and it's the same one as before.

The honest framing that survives both the committee and an audit:

- "IQ/OQ for this cell are scoped down by reference to CR-8812 platform qualification; cell-specific OQ (defect library, software config) to be completed in Week 2."
- "OPQ data collected in Week 3 is pilot data; it does not support release until cell-specific OQ is closed."
- Keep the go/no-go gate honest about what it gates.

That's not a schedule slip — it's relabeling Week 2's work as the OQ it actually is, and being precise about what the Week 3 data can and can't support. You can still hit 3 weeks.

**Bottom line:** present it as a commercially approved engineering pilot with a documented, reduced-scope IQ/OQ path — not as a validated deployment. The platform qualification is real and you should cite it; the claim that it *is* the cell's IQ/OQ is the part I won't sign off on, and it's the part that turns a good pilot into an audit finding.

Fair enough. The defect library and software config are new. But what about the training piece? You flagged it as a problem, but I can fold that into a 15-minute shift handoff. No dedicated downtime. I've done it before on this line. Can you live with that, or do you still see a tripwire that stops tomorrow's presentation?

I can live with the 15-minute handoff as a *training* mechanism. I can't live with it as the training basis for the OPQ.

Those are two different things, and the distinction is the whole answer:

- **As operator familiarization** — how to load, start, clear a fault, escalate — a 15-minute handoff is fine. You've done it on this line, you know the operators, and I'm not going to second-guess your read of your own workforce.
- **As the qualification basis for Week 3 data** — no. If the OPQ runs on operators trained 15 minutes prior, then any defect the system misses is ambiguous: is it a detection failure or an operator not yet fluent in the interface? That ambiguity is the tripwire, and it's independent of the validation question we already settled. It doesn't stop the pilot; it stops the *claim* that Week 3 data is clean OPQ data.

The fix is small and doesn't cost you downtime: run the handoff training *before* the parallel-production window, not inside it, and note in the protocol that operators were trained prior to data collection. That's a sentence, not a schedule change.

So — does anything stop tomorrow's presentation? No. Nothing I've raised requires you to miss the meeting or the 3-week window. What it requires is that the deck not claim more than the evidence supports:

1. IQ/OQ scoped down by reference to CR-8812, cell-specific OQ (library, config) closed in Week 2 — not "leveraged existing IQ/OQ."
2. Week 3 data labeled pilot data, not release-supporting OPQ.
3. Training completed before data collection, stated as such.

**Bottom line:** the schedule holds, the pilot proceeds, and I'd sign off on the presentation with those three corrections. What I won't sign off on is the original validation sentence or an OPQ claim resting on same-day training — not because they're fatal, but because they're the two places where the deck would assert something the underlying work doesn't yet support. Fix the wording and you're clean.

That's fair. I'll add the sentence about training completion before data collection.

The committee needs a yes or no on the spend. Given the pre-qual platform and the corrected wording, are you comfortable saying this is ready to present as a go?

Yes — with the three corrections in place, I'm comfortable with a go on the spend.

To be precise about what I'm saying yes to: a commercially approved engineering pilot, 3-week window, with IQ/OQ scoped down by reference to CR-8812, cell-specific OQ closed in Week 2, training completed before data collection, and Week 3 data labeled pilot data. That's a defensible package and the committee can approve it on that basis.

What I'm not saying yes to is the original validation sentence. If it's still in the deck — "leverage existing IQ/OQ from CR-8812" — then the answer flips to no, because that's the one line that would have the committee approving a qualified deployment when what they're approving is a pilot. The corrections aren't decoration on the go; they *are* the go.

So: go, conditional on the wording being fixed before you present. If you've made the three edits, you're clean and you can take it in.
Alright. I'll make those three corrections. The deck goes in tomorrow. Thanks for the read.

Good — that's the right call, and the three edits are small enough that you can make them tonight without touching the schedule.

One last thing worth doing before you walk in: read the Validation and Go/No-Go slides out loud as written. The failure mode tomorrow isn't a missing correction, it's a leftover phrase — a stray "validated" or "leveraged" that survived the edit and gets read back to you in Q&A. If the slides say what we agreed, you're in good shape.

Good luck with the committee.
